title: Supervision 2 short answers
description: 4 short-answer questions on this week’s lectures, all of them handed in.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 2. There are four short-answer questions, on the control of blood pressure, haemorrhage, hypoxia and heart failure. Answer all four, then hand them in together.

  • Marks. Each question is marked out of 5. Answer in bullet points, and aim for at least 5 separate, precise points: a number, a mechanism or a piece of evidence is worth more than a general statement.
  • Calculations. The calculator is at the top of the page. Show your working, and give units.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Removing the baroreceptors
questions.text:
Explain why removing the arterial baroreceptors (sinoaortic denervation) does not cause a sustained rise in mean arterial blood pressure. What does it change?

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • What the baroreflex does. The carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors fire faster as the pressure (and its rate of rise) increases, and through the medulla they reduce sympathetic and increase vagal activity: negative feedback on ABP, acting within seconds.
  • It buffers, rather than sets. It opposes moment-to-moment changes (standing up, exercise, a sudden noise), but it adapts (resets) to a pressure that is sustained for days, so it can’t hold the long-term level.
  • The evidence. After sinoaortic denervation, the mean pressure over 24 hours returns to near normal, but its variability is much greater: it swings with posture, activity and emotion.
  • What sets the long-term level. The kidneys, through the excretion of salt and water (pressure natriuresis and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system), with the low-pressure (cardiopulmonary) receptors sensing volume. That’s why hypertension is sought in the kidney and in volume control, not in the baroreceptors.
  • A consequence. Without the baroreflex, standing up can cause a large fall in pressure (postural hypotension), and stresses cause large rises.

questions.title: Haemorrhage
questions.text:
Outline the responses to the loss of about 15% of the blood volume, in the order in which they occur.

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes, in order. Each is worth about a mark.

  • The problem. Lost volume lowers MSFP (only the stressed volume, about the last fifth, sets it), so venous return, cardiac output and ABP fall.
  • Seconds. The arterial and low-pressure baroreceptors fire less; pain and fear add drive from higher centres. Vagal activity falls and sympathetic activity rises: heart rate and contractility up, arteriolar constriction (TPR up, sparing the brain and heart), venoconstriction (MSFP back up). Adrenaline, angiotensin II and ADH add vasoconstriction.
  • Minutes. Reverse stress relaxation of vascular smooth muscle; and, with capillary pressure lower, Starling forces favour reabsorption, so 0.5–1 L of tissue fluid moves into the blood (autotransfusion). The haematocrit falls, a more sensitive sign of blood loss than the pressure.
  • Tens of minutes to hours. The kidneys conserve salt and water (renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, ADH, sympathetic nerves), and thirst and salt appetite restore volume by intake.
  • Days. Plasma proteins are replaced by the liver (24–48 h), and red cells by erythropoiesis, driven by erythropoietin from the kidney (5–7 days and more).

questions.title: Two responses to hypoxia
questions.text:
Distinguish the primary and secondary chemoreceptor responses to hypoxia. Why does the cardiovascular response to hypoxia in a breath-hold dive differ from that on ascent to high altitude?

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • The primary response. Low PO2 detected by the carotid and aortic bodies, integrated in the medulla: bradycardia (vagal) and sympathetic vasoconstriction. Strong enough to overcome local metabolic vasodilatation, so blood goes to the brain and heart, which have little sympathetic vasoconstrictor innervation.
  • The secondary response. If breathing is possible, hypoxia also increases the rate and depth of breathing; pulmonary stretch receptors (vagal afferents) then act on the medulla to raise the heart rate, cause venoconstriction (MSFP and so CO up) and a pattern of vasodilatation and constriction favouring vital tissues.
  • Diving. No breathing, so only the primary response: the diving reflex conserves a fixed store of O2 for the brain (heart rate down to 20–30 a minute in cold water in humans; much stronger in seals).
  • Altitude. Breathing continues, so the secondary response dominates: the cardiac output rises, because O2 delivery = flow × content, and more flow makes up for a lower content.
  • The logic. The same stimulus (low PO2) gives opposite responses, depending on whether the lungs are ventilating. (Chronic hypoxia, as in obstructive sleep apnoea, may raise the pressure long term by the same pathways.)

questions.title: Heart failure
questions.text:
Using Guyton’s curves, explain why the body’s normal responses to a low arterial blood pressure can make heart failure worse.

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark. A sketch of the curves helps.

  • The curves. The cardiac function (Starling) curve plots CO against RAP; the venous return curve falls from MSFP on the RAP axis with a slope set by RvR. The output is where they cross.
  • In failure the cardiac function curve is flattened (systolic or diastolic dysfunction), so the curves cross at a lower CO and a higher RAP. Cardiac failure can be defined as a cardiac output insufficient to maintain the body’s target ABP.
  • The normal response to the low ABP: sympathetic venoconstriction and renal salt and water retention raise MSFP (the venous return curve moves up), and arteriolar constriction raises TPR.
  • Why it backfires. On the flat cardiac function curve, a higher MSFP gives a large rise in RAP for a small rise in CO (CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR, so if CO can’t rise, RAP must). High venous and capillary pressures cause oedema, in the lungs and the legs. A higher TPR raises the work and O2 demand of the failing heart, and can lower its output further.
  • So treatment blocks these responses: diuretics and ACE inhibitors (or receptor blockers) lower volume and MSFP, β-blockers reduce sympathetic drive, and vasodilators lower TPR.
